title: Isolation and characterization of iriflophenone derivatives from mango leaves ( Mangifera indica  L.) using high-performance counter-current chromatography and their  in vitro  pancreatic lipase inhibitory activity
content: Pancreatic lipase inhibition is a validated strategy for reducing dietary fat absorption in the management of obesity. Orlistat remains the sole clinically approved pancreatic lipase inhibitor but is associated with gastrointestinal side effects. Natural polyphenolic compounds have attracted interest as potential complementary agents. Although Mangifera indica L. leaves are rich in polyphenolic compounds, the pancreatic lipase inhibitory potential of iriflophenone derivatives from this source has not been systematically evaluated. In this study, a preparative HPCCC method using a biphasic solvent system was developed to isolate bioactive compounds from the methanolic extract of M. indica leaves. The compounds were characterized by ESI-MS and NMR spectroscopy, including mangiferin, iriflophenone-3-C-β-d-glucoside, two galloylated iriflophenone derivatives, a p-hydroxybenzoyl iriflophenone ester, and 1,2,3,4,6-penta-O-galloyl-β-d-glucose (PGG). The pancreatic lipase inhibitory activities were assessed using a fluorometric assay, with 1,2,3,4,6-penta-O-galloyl-β-d-glucose (PGG) demonstrating the highest inhibitory potency, followed by iriflophenone-3-C-(2″-O-p-hydroxybenzoyl)-β-d-glucoside and mangiferin. A reversed-phase HPLC method was developed for identification and purity assessment of the isolated polyphenolic compounds in M. indica leaf extracts. All six isolated compounds were evaluated for in vitro pancreatic lipase inhibitory activity using a fluorometric 4-MUO assay, with PGG (MI-06) demonstrating the most potent inhibition (IC50 = 0.45 µg mL−1), followed by MI-05 (IC50 = 9.04 µg mL−1) and mangiferin (IC50 = 9.26 µg mL−1). This study provides an efficient preparative strategy for isolating iriflophenone derivatives from mango leaves. The findings indicate that the degree and pattern of galloylation influence pancreatic lipase inhibition and support further investigation of M. indica polyphenols as dietary lipase modulators, consistent with reported traditional uses of M. indica. However, further studies including selectivity profiling, aggregation controls, and in vivo validation are needed to assess the translational potential of these findings.
